newsitem.title: INDIA: FORECAST-India TISCO H1 profit seen up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-India TISCO H1 profit seen up.

text.p: Tata Iron and Steel Company Ltd (TISCO) is likely to unveil on Thursday higher than expected first half profits but its growth will be sharply lower than a year ago, brokers and analysts said on Wednesday.
"The market is expecting (net) profit of 2.5 billion (rupees) against earlier consensus estimates of 2.25 billion," said Sanjay Jain, steel analyst at James Capel B&K.
"I'll not be surprised to see that happen."
The company's net profit jumped 132 percent to 2.01 billion rupees in the same period last year.
TISCO is India's largest private steel firm and the flagship of the Tata industrial group. It has one of the world's lowest production costs because of its access to cheap iron ore and coal mines.
Jain saw stronger sales growth and improved efficiency bolstering profits.
TISCO's steel sales rose 8.5 percent to 1.126 million tonnes in the first six months of the 1996/97 fiscal year ended March 31, but this was helped by reducing stockpiles, company figures show.
"There was a reduction of 40,000 tonnes in steel stocks on October 1, 1996 (against year ago)," a company statement said.
Analysts said they had not expected sales volume to grow so much because of depressed market conditions and tougher competition.
"The higher sales is very creditable," Jain said.
Shatayu Mehta, steel analyst at J.M. Share and Stock Brokers Ltd, said TISCO's profits this year will be hit by a new 12.9 percent mandatory tax.
He estimated the tax liability at 320 million to 350 million rupees in the first half, and 900 million to 950 million for the full year.
TISCO, like many Indian blue-chip firms, had avoided taxes by taking advantage of tax breaks on new investments.
Mehta said improved cement capacity utilisation would help the bottom line. Cement sales rose 42 percent to 619,412 tonnes in the first half over the year-ago period, the company said.
Analysts said the firm will see flat volumes growth in the next two years because newer capacities would go on stream only in 1998/99.
"There can be no significant increase in production this year or the next year because there won't be any addition to capacity," said Chetan Ahya, steel analyst at Caspian Securities.
"Profit growth will be driven by better product-mix -- more value-added products," he said.
